description: Southern Italian kingdom (1282–1816) under French Angevin then Spanish Aragonese rule; its Neapolitan court was a major patronage centre for humanist learning, patronising Boccaccio and Petrarch, while its strategic harbours and agricultural wealth made it perpetually contested between the great powers, and its fiscal exploitation by absentee rulers generated chronic social instability.

temporal.notes: Mainland portion after Sicilian Vespers; Angevins then Aragonese

lifecycle_phases.description: The Sicilian Vespers (1282), a massacre of French Angevins in Sicily, splits the Kingdom of Sicily: Sicily goes to Aragon, while the mainland kingdom ('Kingdom of Naples') remains Angevin. The resulting 20-year war ends with the permanent division. The Angevin Kingdom of Naples struggles with the Black Death (1348), baronial revolts, and Hungarian intervention while maintaining Naples as a major commercial center.

Alfonso V of Aragon conquers Naples (1442), reuniting it briefly with Sicily, and makes it a Renaissance court to rival Florence and Milan. His illegitimate son Ferdinand I (Ferrante, 1458–1494) rules shrewdly through complex diplomacy. Charles VIII of France invades (1494) in the first Italian Wars, citing Angevin inheritance claims; Naples changes hands multiple times before Spanish Aragonese forces permanently establish control (1503).

rise_factors.description: Naples's harbor was the finest in the central Mediterranean; the Kingdom of Naples controlled the trade routes between the western and eastern Mediterranean, and the agricultural wealth of Campania, Apulia, and Calabria made it one of the richest territories in Europe
Charles of Anjou's conquest (1266) was papally sanctioned; Angevin kings ruled as papal vassals, giving them legitimacy against Hohenstaufen claims and access to French military networks and finance

Naples and Salerno were among the largest trading cities in the western Mediterranean; customs duties from the Port of Naples and the grain trade of the Apulian hinterland provided the kingdom consistent fiscal revenue

Frederick II's founding of the University of Naples (1224), the first state-founded university in Europe, trained royal administrators; the Angevins maintained this institution, producing the jurists and notaries who ran the kingdom

The fertile plains of Campania and Apulia made Naples a major grain exporter, and the city of Naples was one of the largest in medieval Europe, generating customs revenues that funded Angevin administration.
Robert of Anjou's court attracted Boccaccio, Petrarch, and Giotto, making Naples a major center of the Italian Renaissance's early formation alongside Florence and Avignon.

decline_factors.description: The Italian Wars (1494–1559) turned Naples into a battlefield between France and Spain; the kingdom's strategic position made it attractive to both great powers but gave it no capacity to resist either

The Sicilian Vespers massacre (1282) expelled the Angevins from Sicily, permanently splitting the kingdom and eliminating the island's agricultural surplus; fighting the Aragonese for Sicily drained treasury and military for decades

The Neapolitan barons, never fully subdued, exploited dynastic disputes (especially after 1343) to extract privileges; weak kings like Joanna I could not collect taxes or enforce justice against entrenched feudal magnates
Alfonso V of Aragon conquered Naples in 1442, ending the Angevin dynasty and incorporating the kingdom into the Spanish crown's Italian possessions, which sparked the Italian Wars.
